title: Knowledge Check 4: Lessons 16-20
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 16-20 of the ai-power-user series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Two reports count the same metric differently. Why is that worse than a single wrong number?
options: Because each report becomes slower to produce when definitions differ
Because differing counts mean the underlying data must be missing
Because only one of the two reports can be published at a time
Because the disagreement leaves no basis for trusting either figure
questions.explanation: A single wrong number can be corrected against a known source, but two conflicting figures with no agreed origin leave the reader unable to choose. One agreed source and one written definition matter more than either report alone.

questions.question: A sound compute step produces an impossible metric. Where should you look first?
options: At the exact prompt wording used inside the compute step
At the data shape handed in by the previous step
At the person who reads the final report
At the schedule that started the run
questions.explanation: When the process is sound and the result is still wrong, the input is the suspect: flawed or reshaped data produces flawed output no matter how good the processing is. Checking the handoff before rewriting the step is what finds it quickly.

questions.question: Which report is the weakest candidate for building a workflow?
options: A weekly report that leadership reads and acts on
A monthly report drawn from a stable, agreed source
A one-time analysis for a decision already made
A daily report with a fixed set of fields
questions.explanation: A workflow pays off when a job recurs, keeps a stable shape, and produces output someone acts on. A one-time analysis fails all three, so the structure would add maintenance with nothing to return.

questions.question: A content workflow writes one approved long piece and then repurposes it into several shorter outputs. Where should the human review gate sit, and why?
options: After repurposing, so the gate reviews all the shorter outputs in one pass
Before repurposing, so an unchecked claim cannot spread into every output
Before drafting, so the source material is verified before any words are written
After publishing, so the gate reflects how the audience actually responded
questions.explanation: Repurposing a single source into several channels multiplies whatever it carries, so a wrong claim spreads instead of being caught once. Checking the source piece before the rewrite keeps one error from becoming several.

questions.question: A draft comes back with a confident statistic and no indication of where the number came from. What is the sound way to handle it?
options: Add a prompt rule that forbids the draft from using any statistics
Publish it whenever the figure sounds plausible and matches industry norms
Trace the number to a source you can check, and cut it if none exists
Soften the wording so the claim reads as an estimate rather than a fact
questions.explanation: A plausible, neatly formatted number with no traceable source is fabricated rather than verified. The dependable fix is a checking habit at the review gate, not another prompt rule.

questions.question: Why should a recurring content workflow pull its plan from one shared calendar rather than a personal list?
options: A personal list is slower to update than a shared calendar is
Two versions of the plan drift, so the flow acts on stale data
A shared calendar writes the first draft of each piece automatically
A personal list cannot record which channel a piece is meant for
questions.explanation: A single source of truth prevents divergence. With two versions of the plan, the workflow eventually works from outdated information and drafts cancelled pieces or skips newly added ones.

questions.question: A workflow completes every run without errors and its output is always neatly formatted. Why can it still be failing?
options: Because formatting is the only thing that error logs actually verify
Because a tool that completes a run has by definition produced correct output
Because output is probabilistic, so a clean run can still be wrong
Because failures only appear when a connected tool stops responding
questions.explanation: There is a gap between a workflow running and a workflow working. A model's output comes from a probability distribution, so a run can execute cleanly and be formatted correctly while the answer is quietly wrong.

questions.question: Why are the cases you once had to correct at the review gate the most valuable to keep in a golden set?
options: They are the quickest cases to grade, which keeps the measurement cheap
They are the least mastered, so they fail first when a change degrades it
They make the set larger, and a larger set always measures accuracy better
They prove the bar judges the tool rather than the workflow being measured
questions.explanation: Corrected cases are the ones the workflow has not fully mastered, so they are the most likely to fail first when an update or prompt change degrades the output. That makes them sensitive early detectors of a regression.

questions.question: You have just edited a prompt in a workflow that has a golden set. What should you do before letting the change reach real output?
options: Ship it, since a prompt edit is too small to affect the measured cases
Grade a fresh set of cases drawn only from the newest output
Wait a month so the change has time to settle before measuring
Re-run the same set, and investigate any case that now fails
questions.explanation: The re-run of a fixed, hand-verified set after a change is the regression check. If a case that used to pass now fails, you have found the regression before it reaches anything real.

questions.question: A workflow's input grows past the amount of text the model can consider at once. What is the likely result, and the right fix?
options: The model silently drops or summarizes part of the input, so trim to a summary
The provider returns a rate-limit error, so space the calls out across the day
The model flags the overflow and asks for permission to continue
The workflow stops with a clear error until the input is shortened
questions.explanation: When input exceeds the context window, the model truncates or summarizes it to proceed, and that does not always announce itself. Feeding a compact summary instead of every row keeps the run inside the window.

questions.question: A workflow is refused after several calls in a row, even though plenty of daily allowance remains. What limit was hit, and how should it be handled?
options: A context window limit, so the input should be shortened before retrying
A spend limit, so the monthly cap should be raised before continuing
A rate limit on requests per minute, so pace the calls out over time
A quality regression, so the workflow should be rolled back to a prior version
questions.explanation: Rate limits are measured across requests per minute and tokens per minute, so you can be blocked on requests while your token allowance is untouched. Because the work need not run in one burst, pacing the calls is the fix.

questions.question: Which protection gives the earliest warning against a workflow quietly running up a large bill?
options: A larger context window, so the workflow stops trimming its input
A monthly spend alert that notifies you before the cap is reached
A higher requests-per-minute limit, so bursts finish faster
A smaller golden set, so fewer check runs are made each week
questions.explanation: A spend alert notifies you as tracked spend climbs, while a hard cap stops requests once the limit is hit. A cap you set yourself is the cheapest insurance against a bill that grows without erroring.

questions.question: Which description captures automation bias?
options: Favoring a system's suggestion over correct information elsewhere
Distrusting a system's suggestion even when that output is correct
Assuming every automated system will eventually fail on its own
Preferring to hand a task to a person even when a tool does it well
questions.explanation: Automation bias is the habit of favoring an automated system's suggestion over other information, even when the other information is correct. It appears both as failing to notice a problem and as following a wrong suggestion against the evidence.

questions.question: Which task is the clearest candidate to keep manual rather than run unattended?
options: A low-stakes summary that review would cost more than it saves
A decision that is costly to make wrong and hard to undo
A routine update that a person can reverse as easily as it was made
A recurring job that runs on a fixed schedule with stable inputs
questions.explanation: The test is how much a wrong result costs and how hard it is to undo. When both are high, keep the task manual or let automation run only up to the decision point where a person signs off.

questions.question: A workflow has run for months and saves time on good days, but you keep patching it and re-checking its output. What does an honest review compare before deciding to retire it?
options: The hours it saves on its best day against a fixed monthly budget target
How often it runs against how many teammates happen to use it
The hours it returns against the time spent monitoring and fixing it
Whether it usually works against whether it is occasionally wrong
questions.explanation: Total cost of ownership weighs the hours a workflow genuinely returns against everything spent keeping it alive, and maintenance is often the largest part. When upkeep crowds out the savings, the workflow is a retirement candidate.
